claim: Liu et al. formulate interaction with an unknown linear environment as an output-feedback discounted optimal-control problem and learn an impedance/force policy offline by value iteration from histories of measured inputs and outputs. A contraction result guarantees convergence of the discounted value-function iteration under the paper's augmented linear-system and data assumptions; it does not prove passivity or physical closed-loop stability. A two-DoF simulation approaches the numerical Riccati solution, and a stuffed-toy hardware demonstration shows plausible position and force behavior, but the hardware study has no comparator, repetitions, uncertainty analysis, or safety guarantee and assumes essentially perfect inner-loop trajectory realization.
claim_locator: Section III, augmented system and output-feedback reconstruction
Section IV, value iteration and convergence theorem
epistemic_status: qualified: the learned optimal-control construction and value-iteration contraction are analytical within a linear discounted setting, while interaction performance rests on one simulation and one limited hardware demonstration; stability, passivity, robustness, and safe exploration are not established
problem_and_setting: A manipulator must balance desired trajectory tracking against interaction force while contacting an environment whose constant mass-damping-stiffness dynamics and time-varying equilibrium position are unknown. Only measured input-output histories are used, avoiding direct access to the unobservable environment state.
method_or_mechanism: The robot, desired trajectory generator, and unknown environment-position generator are combined into an augmented linear system. A finite history of measured interaction force, output, input, and reference-endpoint information reconstructs a surrogate state when an observability/rank condition holds. A discounted quadratic cost penalizes velocity, desired-position error, and interaction force. Exploration data are collected first, then an output-feedback value-iteration/ADP algorithm is run offline and the resulting linear feedback kernel is deployed. The discount factor makes the Bellman operator contractive and controls numerical convergence speed.
content_summary: The paper derives a data-based output-feedback optimal interaction controller for a rigid manipulator with an idealized inner tracking loop. It augments known desired-trajectory dynamics with an unknown linear environment-position exosystem, reconstructs the necessary state from N past samples, and learns a quadratic value kernel without identifying all plant matrices. The theorem bounds successive value-function error by the discount factor, so smaller discount accelerates algorithmic convergence while changing the optimization objective. In a two-DoF simulation with a 1 ms step, roughly 100 iterations approach a Riccati benchmark. In hardware, a two-DoF robot with an ATI Mini45 presses a stuffed toy along one axis; 21 offline-learning iterations yield plotted force and trajectory responses. No repeated trials, comparator, or statistical result is provided.
synthesis_role: Represents data-driven optimal impedance adaptation using output histories rather than explicit environment identification. It helps distinguish convergence of an offline Bellman iteration from stability or safety of the deployed human/environment interaction.
development_link: Compared with gradient adaptive impedance laws, the controller optimizes an explicit quadratic performance trade-off from data. Compared with direct model-free policy learning, the augmented linear/LQ structure gives a tractable value-iteration contraction. Compared with robust or passive impedance control, however, the result does not bound energy exchange or uncertainty outside the assumed linear reconstruction model.

evidence.locator: Section II, robot and environment equations
evidence.finding: The environment is modeled as an unknown constant linear mass-damping-stiffness system with a varying equilibrium generated by an unknown linear exosystem, while the robot inner loop is treated as realizing the commanded trajectory.

evidence.locator: Section III, augmented-state and history reconstruction equations
evidence.finding: A finite input-output history replaces the unmeasured augmented state under a rank/observability condition and known order/history length.
The discounted Bellman/value-iteration error contracts by the discount factor; this establishes convergence of the learning iteration, not a passivity or nonlinear closed-loop stability theorem.
For the specified two-DoF linear interaction model, the learned feedback kernel approaches the numerical Riccati solution after about 100 iterations and produces the plotted tracking-force trade-off.

evidence.locator: Section V-B, experimental setup and figures
evidence.finding: A two-DoF robot interacting with a stuffed toy at 1 ms sampling produces plausible trajectory and force traces after 21 offline-learning iterations, without a reported comparator or repeated-trial statistics.

boundary_conditions: The physical derivation assumes perfect inner-loop trajectory tracking, so actuator dynamics and tracking errors are excluded from the learned outer-loop model.
The environment and desired/environment position generators are linear, finite-dimensional, and of fixed order; abrupt switching, hysteresis, impact, and nonlinear friction are outside the proof.
State reconstruction requires a sufficiently long history and an observability/rank condition, plus persistently exciting data for learning.
The convergence theorem concerns discounted value iteration and does not establish Lyapunov stability, passivity, force bounds, recursive feasibility, or robustness of the physical loop.
Learning is performed offline after exploratory data collection; the safety of exploration is not analyzed.
The hardware evidence is one-axis contact with a deformable toy on a two-DoF platform, with no baseline, repetitions, inferential statistics, or out-of-distribution environment change.
The discount factor changes both convergence rate and the optimized long-horizon objective.
assumptions: The augmented input-output dynamics are time invariant over data collection and deployment.
The robot and environment orders used to select the history length are adequate and the reconstructed history state contains the information needed for optimal feedback.
Exploration signals provide sufficient excitation and measurement noise does not destroy the regression/rank conditions.
The quadratic cost meaningfully captures the desired velocity, tracking, and interaction-force compromise.
The learned feedback remains within the domain represented by the offline dataset.
Force and kinematic sensing at the stated sampling period are accurate enough for the history-based controller.

reported: Increasing the trajectory-error weight improves desired-path tracking at the expense of higher interaction force.
Increasing the force/control penalty lowers interaction force while allowing the motion to remain closer to the environment trajectory.
The learning phase is performed offline for safety rather than adapting continuously during interaction.
inferred: Violation of the assumed environment order or observability can make the history state insufficient and bias the learned controller.
A learned discounted optimum may be physically unstable or nonpassive because the theorem does not constrain interaction energy.
Inner-loop tracking error, delays, saturation, and sensor noise can invalidate the augmented linear model used for value iteration.
Offline data may not cover later environment positions or stiffnesses, creating extrapolation risk.
The single hardware trace cannot establish comparative advantage, repeatability, or human-interaction safety.
